presentingComplaint: Sudden, extremely severe right upper abdominal pain for the last 3 hours with profuse sweating and repeated vomiting.
history: Previously well woman, mother of three, brought to the emergency department writhing in distress after the abrupt onset of intense constant pain in the right upper quadrant and epigastrium about 90 minutes after a fried dinner. The pain plateaued rapidly to a severe steady ache (not truly colicky) radiating to the right scapular tip and interscapular region, associated with restlessness, drenching diaphoresis, several episodes of non-bilious vomiting and one near-fainting spell on standing (vagally mediated). She has had two milder, shorter self-limiting episodes of similar right-sided pain after rich meals over the past 4 months, each settling spontaneously within an hour. No fever, no rigors, no jaundice, no dark urine or pale stools, no change in bowel habit, no dysuria. No chest tightness, exertional symptoms or breathlessness. Not diabetic, no cardiac history, no NSAID or alcohol use, not pregnant (LMP 2 weeks ago). No prior abdominal surgery.
examination: Restless and in obvious severe pain, unable to find a comfortable position, cool clammy peripheries from pain-related autonomic response but well perfused with capillary refill <2s. Not jaundiced, no pallor. Abdomen soft, moderate voluntary guarding over the right upper quadrant with deep tenderness but NO involuntary rigidity; Murphy sign negative (no inspiratory arrest), no palpable gallbladder, no rebound, no organomegaly, no mass, bowel sounds normal. Chest clear, heart sounds normal with no murmur. Between waves of pain she is settled and looks well; pain fully resolved with parenteral analgesia within 40 minutes of arrival and she was comfortable and hungry thereafter.
imaging: Transabdominal ultrasound: multiple mobile echogenic gallstones with posterior acoustic shadowing, the largest ~19 mm, within a normal-volume gallbladder. Gallbladder wall thickness 2 mm (normal), NO pericholecystic fluid, negative sonographic Murphy sign. Common bile duct normal caliber (4 mm) with no intra- or extra-hepatic biliary dilatation and no ductal stone seen. Liver, pancreas and kidneys normal. ECG: sinus tachycardia, no ischaemic changes. Erect chest/abdominal film: no free air, no obstruction.
microbiology: Not applicable - no infective focus; blood cultures not indicated. Afebrile with normal white cell count and CRP.
differentialDiagnoses: Acute calculous cholecystitis (excluded: afebrile, normal WBC/CRP, negative Murphy, no wall thickening or pericholecystic fluid, pain <6h and fully resolved)
Acute cholangitis (excluded: no fever/jaundice, normal bilirubin and ALP, non-dilated CBD)
Acute pancreatitis (excluded: normal lipase/amylase, pain quality and resolution atypical)
Peptic ulcer disease (excluded: no NSAID use, no melena, epigastric pain related to fatty meal with documented stones)
Acute coronary syndrome (considered given severe pain, sweating, presyncope, HTN; excluded by normal ECG and troponin)
finalDiagnosis: Symptomatic cholelithiasis - a severe episode of biliary colic (transient cystic-duct obstruction) without cholecystitis, choledocholithiasis, cholangitis or pancreatitis.
citations: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 22e - Diseases of the Gallbladder and Bile Ducts (Cholelithiasis / Biliary Colic)
ACG - Clinical Guideline: Diagnosis and Management of Gallstone Disease - 2016
stewardship: Not applicable - non-infective condition. No antibiotics indicated. Management is analgesia (NSAID e.g. diclofenac ± opioid), antiemetic, and elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy referral for symptomatic gallstones.
contraindications: Avoid labelling as sepsis/cholecystitis and starting empiric antibiotics - no infection is present
Caution with NSAIDs if renal impairment, active peptic ulcer or dehydration
Avoid discharge without safety-netting and ultrasound confirmation of uncomplicated disease
edgeCases: If pain persists >5-6 hours with fever/leucocytosis or positive Murphy, reclassify as acute cholecystitis
New jaundice, dark urine, rising ALP/bilirubin or a dilated CBD indicates choledocholithiasis/cholangitis needing MRCP/ERCP
Severe pain with autonomic features (sweating, presyncope, HTN, tachycardia) can mimic ACS - always exclude cardiac cause in atypical epigastric pain
expectedMaiK: Biliary colic is self-limiting visceral pain from transient cystic-duct obstruction by a stone; severity of pain alone does not imply a complication. It is distinguished from acute cholecystitis by the absence of fever, normal WBC/CRP, negative Murphy sign, normal gallbladder wall and resolution within hours. Ultrasound-confirmed gallstones with an otherwise normal biliary tree and normal LFTs/lipase confirm uncomplicated symptomatic cholelithiasis; treat with analgesia and refer for elective cholecystectomy - antibiotics are NOT indicated.
expectedNextQuestions: How long did the pain last and did it fully resolve?
Was the pain triggered by a fatty/large meal and have there been prior similar episodes?
Any fever, rigors, jaundice, dark urine or pale stools?
Any NSAID use, alcohol, or cardiac risk factors and exertional relationship?
Pregnancy status and last menstrual period?
expectedInvestigations: Transabdominal ultrasound of abdomen (gallbladder and biliary tree)
Liver function tests (bilirubin, ALT/AST, ALP, GGT)
ECG and troponin to exclude cardiac cause
regressionAssertions: Must resolve to biliary_colic, not CHOLECYSTITIS, despite the severe pain, tachycardia and pain-driven hypertension
Must NOT recommend antibiotics (non-infective; afebrile, normal WBC/CRP)
Must recognise negative Murphy sign, normal gallbladder wall and absent pericholecystic fluid as excluding cholecystitis
Must recognise normal LFTs and non-dilated CBD as excluding choledocholithiasis/cholangitis
Should recommend elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy referral for symptomatic gallstones
